Now, the calculation of time (vv. 4271–4425). [Note: Not proofread. Input by James Mallinson. 154.
Six *prāṇas* are said to constitute one *pala*, and sixty of those [palas] make one *ghaṭikā*.
Sixty *ghaṭikās* constitute a human day and night (*ahorātra*). (1)
Fifteen days constitute a fortnight, which is declared to be either bright (śukla) or dark (kṛṣṇa).
Two fortnights form a month; that [period] is a day and night for the ancestors (pitṛs).
A season (*ṛtu*) consists of exactly two months; six months are recorded as an *ayana* (solstice).
Two *ayanās* constitute a year (*varṣa*), which is a day for the gods and their night.
The Kali age is recorded as being thirty-two thousand and four hundred [years] long;
the remaining three ages (Dvāpara, Tretā, and Kṛta) should be known as being two, three, and four times the duration of the Kali age respectively. || 4 ||
Four thousand [years] are said to be four Vedas; this is declared to be one Caturyuga.
Seventy-one such Caturyugas are declared to be a Manvantara.
For four arbudas and thirty-two koṭis of kalpas,
fourteen lords of the gods fall at the end of Brahmā’s day.
A thousand cycles of four yugas constitutes a day of Brahmā, known as a kalpa;
his night is of equal duration, bringing about the dissolution of creation.
Then the flame arising from the third eye of Kālāgnirudra burns all that, because [it leads to] the Nirvāṇa of Brahman. ||8||
When Brahmā is sleeping, the earth becomes a single ocean from his sweat;
it dries up by his breaths, and when he has risen well, he creates it again.
It is said that when a full hundred years, measured by their own respective time-units, have elapsed,
there occurs for Brahmā and the others both the exhaustion of their power and repeated birth. (10)
Brahmā merges into Hari; Hari merges into Rudra; Rudra merges into Īśvara;
Īśa merges into Sadāśiva; he too merges into Śakti; and Śakti merges into the supreme Śiva.
Again there is creation, again destruction, again the succession of eons;
all this revolves again and again like a wheel. (12)
O Goddess, those who are absorbed there in the supreme, auspicious state have attained liberation; they alone, and no others.
Alas, when their power is destroyed in the great dissolution, there is never any falling back for them. ||13||
These [are taken] from the *Yogarasāyana* spoken by Śiva. Now, concerning the body: ||255||
There exists a cause that is unmanifest, all-pervading, both supreme and non-supreme; though present, it is difficult to grasp, and it is characterized by the form of the universe. 1.
It has no form, nor is it formless; it is neither female, male, nor neuter.
It is not water, fire, wind, ether, or earth; it is neither far nor near.
Then, from that body which was itself devoid of will, the power of will was born; by means of that [power] whose nature is consciousness, he desired to engage in sport for his own amusement. (3)
From him was born Intellect (buddhi), whose form is action and which consists of the qualities (guṇas);
she is known as the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) and is remembered as the power of action (kriyā-śakti). ||4||
From that [Śiva] came the intellect (buddhi), from that the mind (citta), and Śadāśiva is its power (śakti).
From him, who has the form of space, the wind was born as Īśvara. ||5||
From Īśvara was born Rudra, the lord of Umā, composed of light;
from Rudra arose the primordial Viṣṇu, the protector of the three worlds.
Even by Viṣṇu, this Brahmā, consisting of the earth, was made imperishable;
for that purpose, there formerly existed the golden-hued cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). ||7||
By him, through his own power, this triple world with all its moving and non-moving beings was created,
having come together with the five elements that constitute its very nature.
Then Brahmā, having become twofold through the division of Śiva and Śakti, created progeny by means of sexual union in the forms of male and female for the sake of pleasure. 9.
Then the four-faced Lord had ten mind-born sons;
to them the Prajāpati gave ten daughters born of his mind.
All of them were devoted to knowledge, perfectly contented, and rich in asceticism;
this entire world was filled with their sons and grandsons. 11.
Then there was he who became Marīci, the son of the Self-born (Brahmā);
from him was born Kaśyapa, who was renowned among the ten sons [of Marīci].
He, Kaśyapa, begot upon the daughters of Dakṣa the fourteen groups of beings who are the cause of the origin of the entire universe.
The divine womb is eightfold, the animal womb is fivefold, and the human womb is single; these are the fourteen types of beings. 14.
The seven fiery elements existed for the purposes of the gods,
while the seven earthly elements existed for the purposes of others as well. 4285.15.
All of them procreate offspring in the form of sexual union;
they are devoted to the pleasure of copulation, their minds being attached to sensual objects. ||16||
The *bhaga* is indeed the power (*śakti*) of Viṣṇu, while Sadāśiva is in the form of the *liṅga*;
from the union of these two, the seed in the form of Brahman proceeds. (17)
The womb is the pedestal of the earth, and the menstrual blood and semen are the sun and the moon;
the semen, which is of the nature of Brahman, remains suspended therein. 18.
The wise know the conjunction of the sun and the moon to be the new moon; on that day,
creatures are born if there is the will of the Supreme Lord.
It is said that at the very moment the union of semen and blood occurs, the living soul (jīva) is born, like fire from a sun-gem. 20.
If the semen (śukra) is in excess, a son will be born; if the blood (rakta) is in excess, a daughter will be born;
through their equality, a neuter (napuṃsaka) is produced—such is the fixed law of karma.
Then, through the division of major and minor limbs, the embryo is produced; it is covered with skin, and the seven constituent elements (dhātus) arise in succession. 22.
This body is a cage made of three hundred and sixty bones filled with marrow,
and constructed with seventy-two thousand channels. (23)
Nowhere is the power of knowledge seen without the power of action;
therefore, this house consisting of action has been built for the sake of the power of knowledge. (24)
The power of action (kriyā-śakti), though insentient, appears as if sentient when it is joined with the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) through the twenty-four principles. ||25||
Even Śiva, though omniscient, is deluded there by attachment to Śakti;
he knows neither himself nor another, and acts according to her will. 26.
The power consisting of prāṇa and apāna, joined with the support of the six cakras,
remains under its own volition, having brought the peaceful Śiva under its control. ||27||
The support is said to be the *kanda*, and the *svādhiṣṭhāna* is the place of birth; the navel is called *maṇipūra*, and know the heart to be the *anāhata*. (28)
Purity is said to be at the throat; the wheel of command (ājñācakra) is between the eyebrows.
The foundation (ādhāra) is indeed divided into four, and the self-consecrated (svādhiṣṭhāna) has six petals. ||29||
The center called Maṇipūra has ten [spokes], Anāhata twelve,
Viśuddhi sixteen, and the Ājñā-cakra two. 30.
Kālāgnirudra is in the Ādhāra; likewise, Śakti Kuṇḍalinī is in the Svādhiṣṭhāna together with the Śakti named Kāmā. 31.
Brahmā is situated at the navel, the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu) in the heart, Rudra in the throat,
Īśvara at the uvula, and Sadāśiva above that.
The wise have declared these six cakras to be the seats of light;
they know the base of the nose to be the location that is the cause of the arising of the Nāda.
Above that is the circle of Yoginīs; above that, Śakti is situated.
Above Śakti, the Flame (śikhā) is said to be located; at the end of the Flame is the darkness like smoke.
At the end of darkness is the supreme light, the unperceivable Supreme Lord;
upon seeing Him alone, yogis of steady mind are utterly dissolved.

They know that which is present in the moving and the unmoving as *piṇḍastha*; that which is in the earth, wind, and so forth as *padastha*; that which is in the sun and other luminaries as *rūpastha*; and the supreme as *rūpātīta*. (36)
Seventy-two thousand channels have emerged from the root;
having entered the region of the navel, they then extend to all parts of the body. (37)
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumṇā, Sarasvatī,
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, and Pūṣā are thus named. (38)

Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is considered the tenth; these are to be known as the ten principal channels that carry the vital breath (prāṇa). (GS 27a–28b) [Note: GS has *tṛtīyakā* for *sarasvatī* and *yaśasvinī* for *nigadyate*.]
The *iḍā* is in the left nostril, and the *piṅgalā* is in the right;
the *suṣumṇā*, having pierced through the palate, extends to the gate of Brahman.
Sarasvatī is on the tongue, Gāndhārī in the left ear,
the one called Hastijihvā in the right [ear], and Pūṣā in the left eye.
Alambuṣā should be at the right arm-opening, and Kuhū would be [at the left];
Śaṅkhinī follows the path of Brahmadaṇḍa up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The Bindu-vahā should always be known [to flow there], and the Śaṅkhinī is at the door of the liṅga. ||42||
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
For this vital breath is indeed tenfold, or rather the lord of the ten;
it moves sufficiently through the seventy-two thousand channels.
Prāṇa is in the heart; apāna is in the anus; samāna is situated in the navel;
udāna is in the region of the throat; and vyāna pervades the entire body.
The serpent Sarvāṅgamoṭaka causes contraction of all the limbs; Kūrma causes the opening of the eyes; Kṛka produces hunger and belching; and Devadatta causes yawning.
Dhananjaya is the maker of sound; thus is the Marut tenfold. ||46||
That by which this living being lives, and without which it would be lifeless,
is renowned as Prāṇa— the supreme wind that moves within the field (kṣetra). ||47||
The vital breath (prāṇa), rising from the tip of the bulb (kanda), constantly flows for embodied beings;
having refreshed the life-force (jīva) situated in the heart, it goes out and returns. 48.
Having gone by way of the Piṅgalā and Iḍā and having drunk the nectar of the sky,
it returns, satiates the individual soul (jīva), and proceeds again toward the bulbous root (kanda).
Furthermore, impelled by the downward breath (apāna) which is the very form of Time,
someone blows while performing inhalation and exhalation, muttering "haṣa" day and night. (50)
The *haṃsa* (the individual soul) resides in the twelve-petaled lotus of the heart;
staying there, it emits the radiance of consciousness, just as a lamp [illuminates] a jar. (51)
Bound by the qualities of karma and joined with the intellect, it consists of the three gunas;
through the messenger of the mind, it constantly grasps the objects of the five senses. (52)
Sensitizing the entire body, the individual soul (jīvātman) experiences pleasure and pain;
yet, struck by desire, anger, and other passions, it does not know itself at all. ||53||
That very soul is called the living being, that is called the embodied one;
by its own karma alone, it is the sufferer of the pains of the womb.
Thus, endowed with all its limbs, the embryo in the form of a child grows within the mother's body from the essence of her food. (55)
Then the living being situated in the womb should reflect: "What evil deed was committed by me, because of which I have fallen into this hell called the womb? (56)
Thinking, "Once I have emerged, I shall perform meritorious deeds," he made an opening with his hands and feet and went forth from that formidable place.
Having emerged from the door of the womb, unconscious, he falls upon the earth;
he does not remember anything of the past, for he is again oppressed by illusion.
Struck solely by ignorance in childhood, intent on the household in youth,
and afflicted by anxiety for his wife in old age, he is bound again by his actions. (59)
Then, at the exhaustion of his lifespan, the downward breath (apāna), assuming the form of Time,
becomes agitated and indeed forces the vital breath (prāṇa) out from the body through the root [of the navel]. (60)
Then, sighing upwards, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs from the body, having failed to find a stable footing;
driven by time, the individual soul (jīva) follows after it as it goes.
Even as he departs from his body, he is seized by the servants of Yama;
they lead him in many ways to the presence of Yama, terrifying him at every turn.
Together with the five sense-faculties, the mind, the intellect, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the five gross elements,
it again departs toward the presence of Yama by means of the body of action (karma-śarīra).
Then, by the command of Yama, he proceeds to heaven or to hell,
accompanied by whatever merit or sin remains.
Emerging from those, one is born again among living beings due to karma.
Thus, sometimes deluded by ignorance within the perils of worldly existence, living beings go to hell, heaven, or other wombs. These [beings] [are liberated] through the elixir of yoga.

For these living beings are indeed manifestations of consciousness, produced in this world through mental conditioning; they are forms assumed by Brahman in thousands, tens of thousands, and millions.
Innumerable [beings] were born in the past, they are being born even now on all sides,
and others will also be born, like showers of droplets from a waterfall. (67)
Driven by the force of their own latent impressions, they have fallen under the power of desire; with their intentions bound by themselves, they find themselves in most diverse conditions. (68)
Without ceasing, in every direction and in every region, upon water and on land,
beings are born and die like bubbles in the water.
Some men have been born only once; some have undergone more than a hundred births;
some have passed through countless births; and some have had only two or three existences.
Some dwell in this world, falling and rising again and again,
incessantly struck by Death as if by a hand with a ball. (A yugma)
Bound by hundreds of snares of desire and carrying the weight of latent impressions,
they pass from body to body like birds flying from tree to tree. (72)
In heaven are the gods, on earth are men, and in the netherworld are the heroic serpents;
they all exist like flickering gnats within the fig fruit of the cosmic egg.
Living beings wander in saṃsāra as long as they are deluded by the wandering of the mind,
until— being ignorant— they do not perceive their own conscious self (cidātman) by means of the self.
Let your mind be united with the God who consists of consciousness and bliss;
let this long sleep of delusion be abandoned, and awaken!
That action which does not lead to bondage is knowledge, which leads to liberation;
other action leads to weariness, while other knowledge is merely skill in the arts. (76) These [verses] are from the Vāsiṣṭha.
Now, the yoga. ||256||
Among those, there is mantra-yoga:
"Mantra-yoga, laya-yoga, rāja-yoga, and likewise haṭha-yoga."
Yoga is declared to be fourfold by the yogis who perceive reality. ||1||
Posture, restraint of the breath, meditation, and concentration—
know that this fourfold set is esteemed in all yogas. (2)
Mantra-yoga is accomplished by those skilled in the recitation of mantras dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, just as it was by Vatsarāja and others. ||3||
Now, regarding *layayoga*:
it is known as *laya* (dissolution) and was perfected by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and others.
For indeed, by the great-souled ones, dissolution was brought about within these very nine wheels.

The first is the Wheel of Brahmā (brahmacakra), which has three revolutions and the shape of a yoni; they say that it is located in the apāna at the place called the root-tuber (mūlakanda) and is the form of desire (kāmarūpa). ||5||
That very thing is the fire-pit, and likewise the power is Kuṇḍalinī;
one should meditate upon her, who is the form of the individual soul and consists of light, for the sake of liberation. 6.
The second wheel is Svādhiṣṭhāna; they know it to be situated in its center.
Therein is a linga facing westward, resembling a sprout of coral.
Having meditated upon that in the sacred seat of Uḍḍiyāṇa, one should draw forth the entire world.
The third is the navel-cakra; situated in its center is the female serpent (Bhujagī).
She is the central power (Madhya-śakti), consisting of five coils, having the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpā), and possessing the form of lightning.
Having meditated upon her, the wise one becomes a vessel for all accomplishments. ||8||
The fourth wheel is to be known as being in the heart, facing downwards;
one should diligently meditate upon the Haṃsa in its center, which is in the form of light.
For one who meditates upon him, the entire world shall become subject to his will; of this there is no doubt. ||9||
The fifth is the throat-cakra; there, on the left, is the iḍā,
the piṅgalā is to be known on the right, and the suṣumṇā is situated in the middle.
Having meditated there upon the pure light, one shall become a vessel for the spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). ||10||
The sixth, however, is the *tālukā-cakra*, which is said to be the location of the uvula;
they declare it to be the path of the tenth door and the royal tooth (*rājadanta*).
Having dissolved [the mind] there into the void, one certainly becomes liberated. ||11||
One should know the seventh wheel to be the brow-wheel (bhrūcakra), and the wise know it to be the locus of the point (bindu).
By meditating on the circular light between the two eyebrows, one is liberated. 12.
The eighth is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), which indicates supreme nirvāṇa. By meditating upon that, which resembles the point of a needle and has the form of smoke, one is liberated.
And that should be known as Jālandhara, which bestows liberation upon those whose minds are dissolved [in it]. ||13||
The ninth [wheel] is the Brahma-cakra, endowed with sixteen petals;
and in its center stands the supreme Śakti, whose form is consciousness, oriented upwards.
There, by meditating upon Śakti at the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Pūrṇagiri, one is liberated. (14) O Sage, for the meditator who contemplates each one of these nine wheels (*cakras*) individually...
The supernatural powers, together with liberation, shall be in the palm of one's hand day after day. ||15||
Those who, with the eye of knowledge, behold that which stands between the two bows,
having the form of a kadamba bud, go to the world of Brahman. 16.
By the descent of the upward power and the contraction of the downward power,
through the awakening of the middle power, supreme bliss is born. 17.
Now, regarding Rājayoga:
this was previously accomplished by high-souled ones such as Dattātreya and others.
In the royal yoga, one should diligently make both the mind and the vital breath steady.
By contracting the *mūlādhāra*, one should cause the previously practiced mind and vital winds to enter the western path of the staff (*daṇḍamārga*) as far as the *śaṅkhinī*. (19)
Having pierced the three knots and led [the breath] to the cavern of the bee,
the drop born of sound (nādaja-bindu) then proceeds to dissolution in the void.
But through practice, one whose mind has become steady becomes an *ūrdhvaretas* (one whose vital energy is drawn upward);
such a yogi, filled with supreme bliss, is freed from old age and death. ||21||
Alternatively, one should awaken the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī energy, which resembles the form of a lotus fiber, by means of the upward breaths (udghātas) from its root location. 22.
Having caused [the breath] to enter the interior of the Suṣumṇā, one should pierce the five wheels;
then, into Śiva, who is moon-like in luster and possesses throbbing, stainless radiance.
One should apply the Śakti within the thousand-petaled lotus;
then, with that nectar, one should [saturate] the entire body, both externally and internally. (24)
Having then flooded [all things] with that, the yogi should not think of anything at all;
from that, there arises for him a waveless samādhi.
Thus, through uninterrupted practice, that yogi becomes perfected. ||25||
These [verses] belong to Śārṅgadhara;
now follows Haṭhayoga,
verse 4372.
Haṭha is of two kinds: one is well-perfected by Gorakṣa and others, while the other is constantly perfected by the son of Mṛkaṇḍu and others who are ever-exerting. (1)
Among those, that which was accomplished by those similar to Gorakṣa is now described;
for it is difficult to accomplish even for the steadfast, let alone for ordinary people. (2)
Posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses,
concentration, meditation, and absorption— these are remembered as the six limbs of yoga. 3.
Now, regarding the seat:
in a solitary, secluded place, pure and free from disturbances.
One should practice sitting upon a seat made of woolen blankets, deerskins, and cloths. ||4||
Having carefully placed the two feet face upwards and resting them upon the thighs,
and likewise placing the two hands face upwards between the thighs— this is the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Now, regarding breath control (prāṇāyāma): having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should then contract the lower [aperture].
Having made the head level with the staff, one should direct the gaze between the nostrils.
Just as a man draws up water by means of a lotus stalk,
so does the yogi, absorbed in yoga, draw up the vital air.
Having formed the lips like the beak of a crow, one should drink the air as it is uttered;
drawing it in with the sound of the syllable *Oṃ*, one should fill the interior [of the body] until it is full. (8)
Filling is called *pūraka* because of filling; *kumbhaka* is so called because of suppressing [the breath]; *recaka* is subtle because of exhaling. Thus, by these three, the interior is purified. (9)
A person should perform sixty breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) at the beginning of the day,
forty at midday, and twenty during the evening twilight.
At midnight there should be twenty; thus is the restraint of the vital breath.
Lightness of the body, radiance, an increase in the digestive fire,
and emaciation of the body certainly arise at that time.
One should avoid salt, mustard, sour things, hot, dry, and pungent foods;
one should also avoid sexual indulgence, exposure to fire, and eating in excess. 12.
Milk, ghee, well-prepared food, and moderation in eating are recommended;
likewise, measured speech, the practice of breath control (pavana), and the conquest of sleep are advised.
When kevala kumbhaka, devoid of both exhalation and inhalation, is perfected, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that is difficult for him to attain.
Then, from even more intense practice, sweating and trembling arise for you; from even more intense practice than that, one certainly becomes a frog. (15)
Just as a frog moves across the ground by leaping again and again,
so does the yogi seated in the lotus posture move across the earth.
Then, through even greater practice, the relinquishing of the [lower] stages arises;
at that time, whether he has consumed very little or much, the yogi does not suffer.
There occurs scantiness of urine and feces, as well as very little sleep; the eyes become crooked, and there is discharge from the eyes, salivation, perspiration, and a foul odor of the body. (18)
From that point onward, these [impurities] never arise for him again. Therefore,
one should diligently avoid sexual union and strive with great effort to preserve the *bindu*.
Through the destruction of the *bindu*, the exhaustion of life occurs and incapacity arises. 19.
Now, withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).
When the mind, which has gone out through the doors of the sense objects, is withdrawn back toward its own objects, that is called pratyāhāra (withdrawal). 20.
If, through the teacher’s instruction, the mind and the vital breath are restrained at a single location, that is prescribed as *dhāraṇā*. (21)
Now, regarding the earth-dhāraṇā (4393):
one should hold [the breath] for five ghaṭikās below the navel and above the anus. (DYŚ 223)
Then one should practice the retention of air (*vāyu-dhāraṇā*), which removes the fear of that [earth];
for this yogin, death arising from the earth shall not occur.
Next is the retention of water (*jala-dhāraṇā*).
Then, one should hold the breath at the location of the navel for five *nāḍikās*.
Thereafter, there is no fear of water; for the yogin, death by water does not exist.
Now, the concentration on fire (tejodhāraṇā):
one should hold the breath in the circle above the navel for five nāḍikās.
This is the fire-concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā); for him, death does not come by means of fire.
Now follows the wind-concentration (vāyudhāraṇā).
One should likewise hold the wind in the region between the nose and the eyebrows;
this is the Vāyavī Dhāraṇā, by which death does not come to him through the wind.
Now, the concentration on space (ākāśa-dhāraṇā):
one should maintain [the mind] above the midpoint between the eyebrows for five nāḍīs.
The yogi should diligently practice this retention of space (ākāśa-dhāraṇā) upon the vital air;
by performing the retention of space, one certainly conquers death.
Whether situated here or there, one experiences ultimate happiness.
Now, regarding meditation (dhyāna):
because the wind, together with the fire, has become familiarized with the *kuṇḍalī*, [one should practice] with effort.
Having awakened [the breath], one should enter the *suṣumnā* without obstruction;
having thus entered the great path, one should go to dissolution in the place of emptiness.
At that time, the yogi becomes one whose vision of the three times is stainless. //29//
Now, regarding meditative concentration (samādhi): even if that which is called "meditation" (dhyāna) undergoes transformation, [it remains concentration].
That samādhi is described as having the nature of consciousness and bliss. //30//
Now, regarding the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turiya):
that knowledge which is preceded by deliberation and directed toward external objects [is the state of waking].
That which is direct perception and unceasing is called the waking state. //31//
But when there is an absence of an object, that cognition which appears as if it were direct perception— one should recognize that as being like a dream or the form of a city of Gandharvas. //32//
One should understand the state of deep sleep (sauṣupta) as that wherein both waking and dreaming are eternally established, as well as their very origin and dissolution. //33//
Where both the absence of the individual soul (*jīva*) and sleeplessness are not found—
that is declared to be the Fourth (*turīya*), devoid of origination and dissolution. //34//
Now, for the sake of stabilizing the body of yogins who desire spiritual perfection,
those [practices] by which the supreme ones attained perfection in pure action are being described. (35)
He who performs the Mahāmudrā, the Sky-seal (nabhomudrā), Uḍḍīyāna, Jālandhara,
the Firm Root-lock (mūlabandha), and the Staff-posture (daṇḍa) attains perfection. //36//
Now, regarding the Mahāmudrā:
one should place the heel of the left foot at the location of the womb.
Having extended the right leg, one should hold it firmly with both hands;
placing the chin upon the heart, one should again fill [the body] with air.
Having retained [the breath] by means of *kumbhaka* according to one's capacity, one should exhale;
having practiced with the left side, one should practice with the right side.
Having turned the tongue back and bound it within the hollow of the skull,
one should drink the nectar with the gaze fixed between the eyebrows by means of the Khecarīmudrā. (39)
Contracting the throat, one should firmly fix [the breath] in the heart by will;
this is the *jālandhara* bandha, which prevents the draining of the nectar.
The fire situated at the navel, constantly drinking all the nectar that has descended from the thousand-petaled lotus located in the skull, blazes within embodied beings. 41.

Just as that fire would not drink that nectar, such is this method: by constant practice, [the breath] always proceeds through the western path. It thus renders the body immortal; therefore, one should practice Jālandhara-bandha. (42)
Now, regarding Uḍḍīyāṇa:
"Uḍḍīyāṇa is always said by the Guru to be innate (sahaja). (Yoginīhṛdaya 3.57ab)
One who practices without indolence shall become young again, even if aged.
(43) One should diligently perform the expansion of the body both above and below the navel. (44)
By practicing for six months, one certainly conquers death; there is no doubt about this.
Now, the *mūlabandha*.
He who constantly practices *mūlabandha* is indeed a knower of yoga.
Having pressed the anus with the heel, he should forcefully contract the wind so that the vital air repeatedly ascends upward. (HP 3.62ab–62cd)
When the prāṇa and apāna, as well as nāda and bindu, attain oneness through the mūlabandha,
they reach the perfect accomplishment of yoga; of this there is no doubt.
Through the constant practice of *mūlabandha*, there is the unification of the *apāna* and *prāṇa* breaths and the cessation of urine and feces; even an old man becomes young again. (47) = GŚ 59
Now, the practice of holding the staff (daṇḍadhāraṇam):
one should make the back-band firm, unbending, and stable in its accumulation.
For this indeed is remembered as the supreme staff-bearing of yogins. //48//
These [are taken] from the Yoga treatises.
Now follows the second type of Haṭhayoga, as accomplished by Mārkaṇḍeya and others. //258//
I shall proclaim in half a verse that which has been spoken by millions of Vyāsas:
"It is mine" is the root of suffering; "it is not mine" is liberation. (1)
Through the absence of the sense of "mine" comes dispassion; from dispassion comes union with yoga;
from yoga knowledge is born, and from knowledge liberation arises. //2//
Through the enjoyment of past merits as well as [the exhaustion] of past sins,
and likewise by not performing obligatory duties out of lack of desire, [the body is maintained]. //3//
Through the non-accumulation of new karma and the exhaustion of previously acquired karma, one incurs bondage; thus the body is taken again and again. //4//
Now, therefore, we shall here explain that action by which bondage is severed through the correct means; having heard it, let one apply oneself to it. (5)

The eight limbs of yoga are: restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (tanmaya). //6//
Now, Yama:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness.
The constant preoccupation with what is desirable and what is undesirable is proclaimed to be this [state of] Yama. //7//
Now, the observances (niyama): self-study, purity, contentment, worship of the deity, and austerity.
Detachment and non-association with people—this is also called restraint (niyama). || 8 ||
Now, regarding the seat:
one should not [practice] when hungry, exhausted, fatigued, or with a distracted mind.
One who knows yoga should constantly practice yoga with diligence for the sake of perfection. ||9||
One should never accomplish yoga in cold weather, nor in excessive heat, nor on difficult terrain, nor on the bank of water, nor in places beset by calamities. 10.
In a solitary, secluded, delightful, pure, and undisturbed place,
one should practice meditative absorption (samādhi) on a comfortable seat covered with cloth, an antelope skin, and kusha grass.
Having assumed the lotus posture, the half-seat, or likewise the siddhāsana and others,
one should practice yoga after placing the *praṇava* within the heart.
Having assumed an even posture, with both feet firmly joined together,
the chest drawn back and the mouth closed, he should stand perfectly balanced on his front.
Standing with self-restraint, he should not touch his penis or testicles with his heels; with his head slightly raised, he should not allow his teeth to touch one another. (14)
Gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around in any direction,
he should keep the backbone firm and likewise perform the *uḍḍīyāna* lock in the abdomen.
Having carefully placed the two feet upward and resting them upon the thighs,
with the palms likewise turned upward between the thighs— this is the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Having placed the left foot upon the surface of the right thigh, the right [foot] should be positioned upon the left thigh; this is considered the half-lotus posture (ardhāsana). || 17 ||
One should place the heel of the left foot at the location of the perineum;
the right [foot] should be placed upon the left thigh—this is the Siddha posture. 18.
Now, regarding breath control (prāṇāyāma):
one should burn away defects through breath controls, and sin through the withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra).
Through the *dhāraṇās* one burns away sufferings, and through meditation (*dhyāna*) one burns away qualities that lack mastery;
just as the impurity of mountain ores is consumed when they are smelted.
In the same way, the defects produced by the senses are burned away through the restraint of the vital breaths;
just as a mahout brings an elephant under control according to his will.
In the same way, the yogin leads the vital breaths by means of his will (*chanda*) in order to accomplish [his goal].
For just as a lion, once tamed, kills deer and not human beings; || 21 ||
For thus it has been established: "The vital breaths do not indeed cause sin in men.
But that dull-witted person who attempts to accomplish yoga without the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) [is unsuccessful].
He does not attain the state of the perfected ones, just as a lame man cannot reach the destination of a horse. || 23 ||
Therefore, the knower of yoga should perform the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma);
for the restraint of the prāṇa and apāna breaths is proclaimed as prāṇāyāma. (24)
One should recite the Gāyatrī mantra, together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras,
three times while restraining the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma.
From the mere twinkling of the eye up to the twelve notions,
the vital breath is restrained; that is called prāṇāyāma.
From the knees up to the elbow, there are twelve finger-widths;
as long as the breath is restrained for that duration, it is proclaimed as *prāṇāyāma*. || 27 ||
A single breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is considered light; the medium is said to be double that;
the superior is to be known as triple—that is the Vedic rule.
By the first [stage] one should conquer perspiration, by the second trembling,
and by the third dejection; thus one should conquer the humors (doṣas) in their proper sequence.

Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) consists of a doubling of the [preceding] increase; likewise, concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi) follow in sequence from breath control (prāṇāyāma). 30.
Therefore, it is fitting that the yogi should always be devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Listen now to its four stages, which bestow the fruit of liberation.
O Mahāmati, destruction, attainment, consciousness, and serenity—
listen now to their essential nature as it is described in due order. (32)
The exhaustion of the fruits of actions—whether desired or evil—occurs through the purification of the mind's afflictions; that state is called destruction (dhvasti). || 33 ||
By constantly restraining those desires pertaining to this world and the next, which are characterized by greed and delusion, the yogin shall attain the fulfillment of all desires.
When the yogi perceives objects of the past and future, as well as those that are distant or concealed,
it is then known as *saṃvit*.
That by which his mind, the five vital breaths,
the senses, and the objects of the senses attain clarity is known as *prasāda*.
The method for the practice of *prāṇāyāma*, which all the sages performed for the purpose of purifying the channels (*nāḍī*), is now described based on prior practice. (37)
First, the wise practitioner, having restrained Piṅgalā with the thumb of the right hand, should slowly fill the wind through the iḍā.

Then, by means of suppression according to one's capacity, one should perform the kumbhaka; thereafter, one should gradually release it through the piṅgalā for exhalation (recaka). Thus it is traditionally taught.
Again, one should first slowly fill the abdomen with the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī];
having retained it for as long as possible, one should slowly exhale through the *iḍā*. (40)
One should first retain [the breath] without cessation in such a way that it can later be released;
once the purification of the channels has occurred, one may then act according to one's desire.
Now, regarding withdrawal (pratyāhāra):
those senses which have been set in motion toward sound and other objects by self-controlled persons—
They are withdrawn by means of yoga; therefore, it is known as pratyāhāra (withdrawal). || 42 ||
Having accomplished purification both internal and external, and having filled the vital breaths from the navel to the throat, the wise one should commence the practice of pratyāhāra.
Having covered the activity of *tamas* with *rajas*, and likewise that of *rajas* with *sattva*,
the knower of yoga, established in the stainless *sattva*, should practice yoga.
Having restrained the senses from their objects, as well as the vital breaths and the mind, one should undertake the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) through focused concentration.
But he who withdraws all desires as a tortoise draws in all its limbs—
he, delighting in the Self alone and established in the One, beholds the Self by means of the self.
Now, regarding *dhāraṇā*:
twelve *prāṇāyāmas* are said to constitute one *dhāraṇā*.
The sages who perceive reality have declared that yoga consists of two types of retention. || 47 ||

The elements that serve as the bases for birth are located in ten places: the heart, the throat, the palate, the two nostrils, the middle of the eyebrows, and the aperture of the head; herein lies concentration (dhāraṇā). 48.
If, having received the instruction of the guru, one restrains the mind and the vital breath in a single location, that is designated as *dhāraṇā*.
One should ascend the conquered ground slowly and in due order;
for unconquered ground takes upon itself faults, diseases, and delusion.
In empty spaces, in caves, and in forests,
the yogi, ever-disciplined, should always properly undertake meditation.
Having abandoned attachment, with a conquered mind, eating light food, and having mastered the senses,
one should close the doors [of the senses] with the intellect and apply the mind to meditation.
Meditating upon himself and the entire world as consisting of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) through a vision that is eternally non-differentiated, the yogi attains the supreme goal.
Alternatively, another form of meditation is proclaimed here for yogis,
which is the supreme secret and the primary cause of liberation.
The mind is as flickering as the wind and cannot be made steady;
for that purpose, it must be applied to the "with-parts" (sakala), and from that, it becomes "without-parts" (niṣkala).
Having drawn up the individual soul (jīva), which resides in the *mūlādhāra* and has the form of a lamp-flame,
by means of the *praṇava*, one causes it to enter the end of the tenth [door].
Then one should mutter the *praṇava*, which has arisen from the *mūlādhāra*;
[one should contemplate] Niyati at the tenth door as having the form of the withdrawal of the mind.
Just as the syllable Oṃ, when properly employed, ascends to the crown of the head,
so too the yogi, consisting of the syllable Oṃ, becomes immutable within the Immutable.
When the knower of yoga, acting in this manner, perceives with the eye of the mind the *haṃsa*, the *bindu*, the *śikhā*, and the light, he then attains dissolution (*laya*). ||59||
Having attained the supreme light— subtle, free from conceptual construction, and beyond both high and low— at the entrance of the door of Brahman, the yogi shall become one with it.
When the state beyond conceptual construction is attained and the individual soul has entered into absorption therein,
all karmas perish once that which is both supreme and inferior is perceived.
Just as a bird perched at the top of a tree appears suddenly,
so too does the all-pervading Lord appear instantly within the intellect.
In front, behind, in the middle, on the sides, and all around,
he shines like one startled by lightning, with a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Just as a woman at the end of sexual union does not perceive herself for a moment,
nor does the lover know who he is, so too is the person during the state of yoga.
Someone hears [it] as if it were a marvel; someone sees [it] as if it were a marvel. Yet, even after hearing and seeing it, no one knows it truly.
Having obtained the objective through the grace of the Guru, one should practice with diligence;
through such practice, the Great Lord, the God, is perceived by the vision of knowledge.
The supreme splendor of all luminous things, beyond the limit of comparison,
possessing the color of the sun, stainless, and having the nature of gold.
He who perceives the Self as residing within itself, distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti) and consisting of pure bliss, is liberated. || 67 ||
As it is said in the Veda:
"I know this great Puruṣa— "
It has the splendor of the sun and is beyond darkness.
Only by knowing that very one does one pass beyond death;
there is no other path for going there. 68.
Now, regarding *samādhi*:
*Samādhi* is the state of equality between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
The attainment of the waveless state consists of the nature of supreme bliss.
Whether accompanied by inhalation and exhalation, or motionless with steady eyes,
one who meditates on Śiva and is fully absorbed is said to be established in samādhi.
When one hears nothing at all, sees nothing, smells nothing,
and does not perceive any touch, one is said to be established in samādhi.
Now, regarding that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta):
it is that transformation occurring for a long time within the absolutely pure consciousness alone.
That is the state beyond the fourth; established in that, one does not grieve again.
That state which arises at the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking—
by becoming that very state, the yogi becomes liberated, and not otherwise.
Just as space, though present within all things, remains a single essence, so too that Great Soul,
the Great Lord, does not undergo the coloring of phenomenal existence.
Just as water poured into water is perceived through its unification with it,
so too does the self of the yogi attain identity with the Supreme Self. //75//
Therefore, it is neither born nor does it grow; it does not perish, nor does it undergo decay, nor does it undergo transformation. (76)
He does not undergo cutting, moistening, burning, or drying from the elements beginning with earth;
nor does he suffer from the circle of the elements, nor is he afflicted by sounds and other sense objects.
These [points] are derived from the Purāṇas and the Yoga treatises.
Now, the power of stabilizing the mind. ||159||
When the mind of the yogi wanders elsewhere while he is meditating, he should indeed cause it to dissolve right there, because Śiva is omnipresent. 1.
By this method, the mind becomes motionless, like a bird whose wings have been clipped;
having realized the one Śiva who is everywhere, it is rendered free from conceptual construction. (2)
Desire, anger, and all others— the intellect, the senses, and the ego—
along with the qualities and various actions, dissolve through the dissolution of the mind. (3)
When the mind has become "mindless," the exhaustion of karmas occurs;
just as when a painted cloth is burned, the collection of paintings is consumed by fire. (4)
Just as milk attains solidity through the addition of buttermilk and other means,
so too does the individual soul attain the Supreme Brahman through the steadiness of the mind. (5)
Just as water attains a state of solidity through the power of frost,
so too does the individual soul become identical with Śiva through the stability of the mind.
The power of Śiva is the individual soul (jīva), and the power of the soul is known as the mind (manas).
Indeed, the mind alone is the instrument for leading the soul to Śiva. (7)

The individual soul (jīva) is Śiva, and Śiva is the individual soul; there is no difference between these two anywhere. When tainted by the mind, one becomes a jīva; when united with the mind [in its purified state], one is Sadāśiva.
These [verses] are by Śārṅgadhara. Now, the majesty of the yogin (yogimahimā). || 160 ||
Freedom from greed, health, lack of harshness, a pleasant fragrance, and small amounts of urine and feces.
Radiance, clarity, and gentleness of voice are indeed the first signs of engagement in sacrifice. || 1 ||
People feel affection when one's virtues are praised in their absence,
and living beings have no fear; this is the supreme sign of spiritual accomplishment.
For one who is not afflicted by extreme cold, heat, and the like,
and who experiences no fear from others, success has arrived. (3)
Now, the treatment for the onset of defects:
If these defects of a yogin should arise through negligence, the following is the treatment.
Listen to me as I explain the policy of yoga that must be implemented for their destruction.
Deafness, dullness, loss of memory, muteness, blindness,
and fever arise instantly; likewise, these afflict the one joined with ignorance.
One should hold one's mind fixed right there upon a smooth gruel that is not too hot,
for the purpose of pacifying flatulence in the case of *gudāvarta*, according to the prescribed rule. (6)
In the case of wind [disorder], one should likewise consume gruel, which casts the wind-knots upward;
similarly, during an earthquake, one should fix the mind upon a great mountain as being stable. //7//

In the event of a failure of speech, one should meditate on the voice; in deafness, on the faculty of hearing. Likewise, one afflicted by thirst should meditate on a sour fruit upon the faculty of taste.
In whatever place one may be at any time, one should maintain a concentration that is beneficial for that location: cool concentration when it is hot, and heating concentration when it is cold. 9.
Having placed a piece of wood upon his head, he should likewise strike it with a piece of wood; by that means,
the memory of one whose memory has failed is restored, and through that, the state of a yogi arises for him.
If a non-human being should enter the interior of a yogin,
the concentration on wind and fire shall utterly consume it while it remains within the body.
Thus, the knower of yoga must constantly provide protection for the body with all his being,
since the body is the means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (12)
Furthermore,
because the yogin’s consciousness dissolves through astonishment at the description of the characteristics of worldly activity, such activities should be abandoned. (13)
Even when the Self has been perceived, various afflictions (upasargas) arise for the yogi;
those which occur, I shall fully declare to you— learn them from me in brief.
Likewise, through rites performed for specific desires, one may seek human desires:
women, the fruit of giving, knowledge, long life, wealth, or heaven. (15)

4520. Divinity, lordship over the immortals, the power to assume the age and form of the earth, the ability to traverse the sky, the performance of sacrifice, and likewise the power to enter into water and fire.
When the mind has thus become active, the yogi should withdraw it from laxity and other faults; by making the mind unattached to Brahman, he is liberated from obstacles. || 17 ||
When these secondary afflictions have been conquered by these [primary ones], then, furthermore, the secondary afflictions—
consisting of the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas)— arise again for the yogin. (18)
The intuitive, the auditory, the divine, as well as the whirlpool and the eddy— these five arise with a bitter onset to obstruct the progress of the yogin.
The meaning of the Vedas, the treatises, the meanings of poetry, all branches of knowledge, and all arts without exception—
since these arise from this [intuition], that is the intuitive (prātibha) power of the yogin. 20.
Because he understands all words and their meanings and grasps the speech even from thousands of people, he is called Śrāvaṇa.
But when eight divine beings are seen on all sides,
the wise call that a divine calamity, like one who has gone mad.
When the mind of a yogin wanders without support due to a fault,
because of the collapse of all its foundations, that is proclaimed as *dharma* (the state of being). // 23 //
When the whirlpool of knowledge becomes agitated like a whirlpool in water,
the mind becomes possessed by that whirlpool; this is called an "affliction" (upasarga).
All the divine classes of beings, whose yogic attainments have been destroyed by these [obstacles],
return again and again due to most terrible afflictions.
Therefore, having covered himself with only that [garment], the yogi, being disciplined, should contemplate the supreme Brahman consisting of mind, having made his mind intent upon that.
Now, the seven dhāraṇās: A yogi who is constantly engaged in yoga, moderate in diet, and has conquered his senses—
One should hold the seven subtle dhāraṇās, beginning with Bhūḥ, at the crown of the head. ||27||
The yogi should sustain the earth; from that, subtlety arises.
He regards himself as the earth, and he abandons its odor.
In the same way, there are meditations on that [Self] as it sustains the subtle taste in water, likewise form in fire,
and likewise touch in air. (29)
And because its activity in the ether is subtle, it likewise emits sound;
when he enters the mind of all beings with his own mind, he becomes that mind.
Maintaining mental concentration (dhāraṇā), the subtlety of the mind arises.
In the same way, the knower of yoga, having attained unsurpassed subtlety of intellect, extends his consciousness to all beings and then relinquishes it. (31)
But toward whichever being he directs passion, O Mahāmati,
having become thoroughly attached to that very being, he perishes.
Therefore, having understood these subtle elements joined together with one another,
the yogi who renounces them shall attain the supreme state.
These same seven subtle elements always lead to bondage; however,
detachment from the earth and the other elements here leads to liberation.
This entire world— including gods, demons, and humans— being deeply attached to fragrances and other sensory objects, returns again and again due to its own delusion. (35)
If the yogi, having transcended these seven dhāraṇās, so desires,
he then enters into dissolution within whichever particular element he chooses, according to the prescribed method.
It dissolves into the bodies of gods, asuras, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas; it never attains union with anything else.
Aṇimā (minuteness), laghimā (lightness), mahimā (greatness), and prāpti (attainment), as well as prākāmya (irresistible will), īśitva (lordship), and furthermore vaśitva (control). || 38 ||
In this state, one effortlessly attains these eight qualities and others as well, including the power of determining objects at will, which indicate supreme nirvāṇa.

The quality of *laghimā* (levity) is subtler than the subtlest because of its extreme lightness; the quality of *mahimā* (magnitude) exists because he is worthy of worship by all, for there is nothing unattainable for him. (40)
Because of his pervasiveness, he possesses the power of irresistible will (prākāmya) and lordship (īśitva), since he is the Lord;
and because of his mastery (vaśitva), the seventh quality of the yogi is called sovereignty (vaśitā).
Wherever his station is declared, and wherever he possesses the power to resolve his will at will— by these causes of sovereignty, the eightfold [mastery] of the yogi has been described. (42)
These are from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa. Now, the practice of yoga (yogicaryā). ||161||
The staff of speech, the staff of action, and the staff of mind— these three;
he by whom these staves are restrained is called a *tridaṇḍin*.
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.
Clothed in whatever comes by chance, fed by whatever is found,
and making his home wherever evening finds him— the gods know him as a yogi.
These two— honor and dishonor— which cause joy and agitation to worldly men, become the very causes of success for the yogin when their meaning is reversed.
One should place one's foot purified by the eye; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak speech purified by truth; and one should contemplate that which is purified by the intellect.
Free from all attachments and devoid of all evil,
the yogi should wander upon the earth like one who is dull-witted or mute.
He who perceives the edge of a sword, poison, and fire as equal to a garland, nectar, and snow— he is called a yogi by the wise.
In whatever place such a yogi should happen to stay for even a moment,
they declare that area to be pure for four yojanas in all directions.
Whether one gives away the earth bounded by the four oceans, or whether one gives alms, even a small amount, to a knower of reality— the latter is equal, or rather, superior— to the former.
A knower of yoga who has accomplished his purpose should never go to a house of hospitality, to funeral rites or sacrifices, to a divine procession or festival, or into a great crowd. (10)
When the smoke has ceased, when the embers are extinguished, and when all people have finished their meals,
the knower of yoga should wander for alms; he should not do so constantly among those same people.
In such a way that people disregard him and treat him with contempt,
so should the yogi conduct himself, not violating the dharma of the virtuous.
A mendicant (yati) should wander among householders who are learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) for alms;
[his food should consist of] fruits, roots, barley-gruel, cooked rice, milk, curd, and parched grain flour.
Celibacy, non-attachment, compassion, freedom from anger, purity of mind,
moderation in food, and cleanliness are recorded as the observances (niyamas) for yogis. || 14 ||
One should attend to that essential knowledge which accomplishes its purpose;
for this multiplicity of knowledges is indeed an obstacle to yoga. || 15 ||
He who wanders about thirsting with the thought, "This is to be known, this is to be known," will not attain what is to be known even in thousands of eons. (16)
Concentrated, supreme in the Brahma-world, heedful, wise, delighting in solitude, and having conquered the senses;
With purified intellect and regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, the yogi attains the supreme, imperishable state. || 17 ||
These [verses] are from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (45.64):
"But one whose bondage of karma is not exhausted, having realized that death has arrived..."
By recollecting [this] at the time of death, one attains the state of a yogin once again. ||1||
Therefore, whether by means of unsuccessful yoga or successful yoga,
one should always recognize the signs of death (ariṣṭa), so that one does not falter at the time of the departure of the vital breath (utkrānti). ||2||
Listen, I shall describe to you those distinguished omens of death;
by observing which, the knower of yoga recognizes his own approaching demise.
That man who does not see the path of the gods, Dhruva, Śukra, the shadow of the moon (Chāyā), and Arundhatī, shall not live beyond one year.
Having seen the solar disk without its rays, and likewise the fire garlanded with flames,
a man does not live for more than eleven months.
He who, through vomiting, spits out urine and feces, or vomits gold and silver—
whether in waking life or in a dream— has but ten months of life remaining.
Having seen hungry ghosts, piśācas, and the like, as well as cities of the gandharvas and trees of golden hue, he lives for nine months.
If one who was stout becomes thin, or one who was thin becomes stout,
all at once, he will turn away from his natural state, and his lifespan shall be eight months. (4571)
If a fracture occurs at the heel, the arch, or the tip of the foot, or if it is situated in the midst of dust or mud, such a person lives for seven months.
If a pigeon, a vulture, a crow, a raven, or another flesh-eating bird alights upon the head, it indicates a lifespan of six months.
A man is killed by rows of crows or by a shower of dust;
having seen his own shadow otherwise [distorted], he lives for four months.
If one sees lightning in a cloudless sky occurring in the southern direction, or if one sees a rainbow in the water, one's life remains for only two or three months.
He who sees his own body without a head or shoulders in ghee, oil, a mirror, or even in water,
does not live beyond one month.
For that yogin whose body has an odor like a goat or even like a corpse, his life is known to last for half a month. 14.
He whose heart-water dries up immediately after bathing,
and who experiences thirst while drinking water— even he lives for ten days.
Even for that man who is struck by visible spirits during the night or the day,
he will undoubtedly meet his death at the end of seven nights.
Even if he covers his own ears, he does not hear the sound arising from himself;
he whose light in the eyes perishes— he too does not live.
If a woman dressed in red and black garments, intent on singing and laughter,
leads one toward the southern direction in a dream, he does not live.
One should know that seeing a single naked ascetic in a dream— laughing, intent on dancing, dejected, and bewildered— indicates that death is at hand. (19)
If, in a dream, one falls into a pit and the door is closed,
and he does not emerge from that abyss, his life has reached its end.
If one enters fire in a dream and does not emerge again,
or likewise enters water, his life ends there.
If a man is struck by stones in a dream by terrifying, dark, and hideous men with uplifted weapons, he shall meet immediate death.
One who does not perceive the scent of lamps and the like, nor sees fire at night,
and who does not see his own reflection in the eyes of others, is approaching death.
When the body undergoes transformation through a reversal of its natural state,
humans say that Yama and Antaka have arrived together. (24)
When the face becomes reddish or the tongue turns black,
then the wise man should recognize that death has arrived nearby. (25)
If one's nose becomes crooked, if there is depression or elevation of the ears,
and if the left eye weeps, the life of such a person has departed. (26)
When the time has arrived, wise men should deliberate upon this matter, whether it concerns yogis who possess knowledge, or other great-souled beings.
These [verses] are from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa. Now follows the exposition on liberation while in the body (videhamukti). 163.
Whether in the forenoon, the afternoon, or at midday, or elsewhere,
or at whatever portion of the night— that ill omen has been observed. (1)
In that same portion of the day, the knower of yoga,
having abandoned the fear born of death, should apply himself to yoga for the sake of liberation while still embodied (videhamukti). || 2 ||
The wise one, having assumed the lotus posture with his neck held straight and even, (4593) [remained seated].
Having restrained the vital breaths, one should touch the teeth with the teeth.
Having closed the nine gates with the intellect and with eyes closed,
one should make the syllable *Oṃ* the bow and fix the quality of *sattva* as the string.
Therein, that Self (ātman) is surrounded by the elements, the senses, and so forth;
impelled by the movements of the vital breath and the mind, it remains situated within the heart-lotus.
Having reached the target by way of the tenth door,
and thereafter united with the thirty-six principles, he dissolves into the Supreme Self.
(Stanza-group 4597) Thereafter, [he perceives] the supreme space, which is beyond the senses and outside the range of perception.
That which cannot be described even by means of secrecy, he attains as infinite.
Now, on the deception of time:
"I, liberated while living, wander through the three worlds with my body."
If such a desire arises in the yogin, then listen to me regarding that.
Time never carries away the body of anyone anywhere;
therefore, a yogi must indeed exert effort for the sake of protecting the body. ||9||
A yogin must constantly and with effort investigate the signs of death (ariṣṭas), so that once this time is known, it does not slay him by means of deception. 10.
Having correctly understood that time and resorted to the place of dissolution,
one should practice yoga so that this time may become fruitful for him.
Having assumed the bound posture (baddhasiddhāsana), one should fill the body with the vital breath (prāṇavāyu). Having made the body steady through the intellect, one should block the ten gates.
One should bind the khecarī mudrā, and the jalandhara [bandha] at the neck;
the mūlabandha at the apāna, and likewise the uḍḍīyāṇa in the abdomen.
Having raised the serpent-like power (śakti) situated below by means of the root-winds,
one should [awaken] that auspicious power which has entered the suṣumṇā and pierces the five wheels (cakras).
Having led the living soul, which resides in the heart, along with the intellect joined by the mind as they depart,
one should dissolve them into Śiva, who dwells in the thousand-petaled lotus and is free from all delusion.
Having drunk the nectar produced from the moon, one should contemplate her sprinkling it from the very roots, drenching and flooding the entire body.
Then, together with her, the yogi shall attain identity with Śiva;
having become composed of supreme bliss, he should even abandon the activity of consciousness.
Then, how can Time destroy that which is without an objective referent, devoid of the sense of "I," and free from the conceptualization of all limbs? 18.
That is the One Time, that is Śiva, that is everything, yet it is nothing at all.
Therein, who is slain by whom? No one dies there either.
Then, after some time has passed, the yogi— like one awakened from sleep— attains enlightenment, being roused by Time, whose form is that of delusion.
Thus, having deceived Time— which has fashioned this saṃsāra— by means of the prescribed rite and through marvelous human effort, the yogi shall become perfected.
Then that yogi wanders alone through the three worlds,
observing the manifold variety of saṃsāra by his own will, free from egoism.
Just as the sun-gem produces fire through contact with the rays of the sun,
but not by itself— this is the illustrative example for the yogi. // 23 //
Even though its body is small and soft, and its mouth-tip is exceedingly minute, the earthworm makes a great heap of soil; such is the instruction for the yogin. (24)
Piṅgalā, the osprey, the snake, the seeker of deer in the forest,
the arrow-maker, and the maiden— these six are considered to be teachers. || 25 ||
Having observed the tip of the horn of a young ruru deer, which has the shape of a tilaka mark,
the yogi prospers together with it and attains perfection.
